title: UPDATE: Expert says meteor shower is rare sighting

content:
SIOUX FALLS, S.D. (KELO) -- A viewer shared a video of possible space debris in the sky around 2:45 a.m. Tuesday morning.

Larry Browning, SDSU Professor Emeritus of Physics, says the sight is most likely part of the Chi Cygnids meteor shower.

The sky lit up early Tuesday morning while most people were still sleeping.

"I walked out and it kind of got my eye up in the sky, and I didn't really know what to think, what it was," said Riley Bussinger, who witnessed the meteor shower. "You know, I don't know anything about astronomy or meteors or asteroids or whatever."

Riley Bussinger was leaving for work when he spotted the bright lights up above.

"I got to thinking about how, you know, what are the odds that I just walked outside the same time it was going by?" said Bussinger.

As it turns out, the event was even more rare than he thought.

"It seems most likely that it was an event that came along with this particular- and usually we don't pay too much attention to it- the Chi Cygni meteor shower," said Larry Browning, SDSU professor emeritus of physics.

A few factors contributed to the event being more visible than usual. At that time of night, the rotation and motion of the Earth are going the same direction, making us move faster through space.

"That usually gives you a more spectacular meteor shower," said Browning. "And you can see in the video where the thing was getting really hot and behind it, it was trailing other little specks. And it was probably debris coming off of the main element."

The phase of the moon also accentuated the view of the meteor shower.

"It was near a new moon," said Browning. "And so, the moon wasn't bright and making the meteor less intense. So, you really saw it against the black sky. So, it was almost a perfect storm, if you will."

A perfect storm that not very many people had the opportunity to witness.

"It just seems like the odds were next to zero," said Bussinger.
